cells.tense: You are holding what you know steady, and the timing of the telling is yours.
cells.ask: Say one true thing to the person in front of you, before you've checked whether it will land.
cells.core:
There are two people in the room and you're actually with them. You can feel what they mean, not just hear the words, and most of the time you're willing to wait instead of rushing it into the air. That waiting isn't doubt. It's you keeping the words back until the moment they're supposed to land.

When the moment comes, say it plainly, once, without checking it against their face first. That's the whole exercise — speaking is only half of it. It doesn't need a rehearsal, and it doesn't need to be certain to be true. Say it and stay in the room while it settles. What telling needs is already in you; the pause has just gotten comfortable enough to keep.

cells.tense: You will have examined what you know so many times that the moment will pass unspoken.
cells.ask: Say one true thing today and speak it without waiting for it to be perfect.
cells.core:
You can see what's true between you and someone else, but you're not saying it. Instead you're running it forward — checking the phrasing, imagining how it lands, testing the other version, then the version after that. Nothing is wrong with what you see. It's that you keep holding it, and the holding has gone on too long. Somewhere ahead you're waiting for the moment it will be safe to speak, and the moment keeps moving because you keep it moving.

Say one true thing today, in the size it actually is. It will be imperfect and that's what lets it land. The stopping is the point — not a better version of the sentence. Say it before you're sure. That's a different exercise than what you've been doing, and it ends the waiting.

cells.tense: You held what you knew and didn't say it, and you're still standing there.
cells.ask: Tell someone one thing you notice in them, the first thing that comes.
cells.core:
You're quiet now, and you weren't always. Somewhere along the way you stopped saying the thing you saw, and you've kept the silence since. What you notice didn't go anywhere — you still catch what people mean, what they don't say, what they need. You just don't say it out loud. So the room gets your attention and none of your voice. You're present in body and absent in the part that speaks.

Say what you notice. Not a verdict, not the big version — one thing, early, before it's polished. Notice what happens next, because that's where the real information is. Connection runs on small true moments, and they don't wait. The telling will feel unfinished the first time. It won't need to feel finished to work.

cells.tense: You are already reading the room correctly and calling it nothing.
cells.ask: Name one thing you noticed about someone this week and say it like it's yours.
cells.core:
You're already acting on what you see. You read the room, you catch what people don't say, you shape your words to fit who's in front of you — and all of it runs without a claim, like it happens on its own. Something real is at work here, and the person it comes from isn't getting any of the credit. Said plainly, it sounds like bragging; so it stays unspoken and keeps working quietly.

Say one thing you noticed this week, out loud, and say it like it's yours — not like the room decided it. The catch you made was yours. That's the whole of it. Fair exchange between two people needs what you offer to be visible, and you've been offering without saying so. Say it once, then let them answer.

attempts.check: The record gives Reflection's balance as inner knowing that lands without argument, but says nothing about whether this person has anyone to be in step with; the reader could reasonably say the alignment and mutual understanding are mine, not theirs. The ask still works if my read is wrong, because saying one true thing plainly is useful whether or not their knowing is already clean, and it costs nothing to try. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line suggesting their knowing has always been accurate — so I've kept the telling unnamed and the balance framed as what the pause is for, only when the time comes.
